paragraphs: Label ranking asks a model to predict an ordering of labels, so its output has more structure than a single category or number. This paper treats that task as structured output regression. It represents rankings as vectors, learns to predict those vectors using a least-squares surrogate loss, and then converts the predictions back into rankings.

The choice of vector representation is central. A regression output does not automatically correspond to a valid ordering, so recovering a ranking can become the expensive part of the method. The paper studies embeddings that help in different ways: some yield consistent estimators, while others make this decoding step straightforward. These are alternative benefits of the representations, rather than a claim that every embedding provides both.

The authors also discuss extending these representations to incomplete or partial rankings, where an entire ordering is unavailable. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the approach's usefulness. The contribution is a framework connecting ordinary regression machinery to ranking prediction, with explicit attention to both statistical behavior and the practical difficulty of decoding.
neurips-2018-a-structured-prediction-app.tldr: The paper predicts label rankings through vector regression, using ranking embeddings that support consistency or simplify decoding.

paragraphs: A nonconvex optimization problem can have local minima that look optimal nearby but are worse than solutions elsewhere. This paper studies continuous objectives without such misleading minima, calling them global functions. Their defining feature is that every local minimum is also global, even though the objective need not be convex or differentiable.

The authors develop mathematical tools for analyzing this class. They establish a result analogous to the uniform limit theorem for continuous functions and examine properties involving function composition and changes of variables. These tools matter because an objective's useful structure may become easier to establish after expressing it through other functions or coordinates.

The theory is applied to a class of nonsmooth, nonconvex problems arising in tensor decomposition. The authors show that these objectives are global functions, providing a guarantee relevant to using the ℓ1 norm for resistance to outliers. The guarantee concerns the analyzed class of objectives: it establishes the absence of inferior local minima there, rather than claiming that every nonconvex problem using an ℓ1 objective has a benign landscape.
neurips-2018-a-theory-on-the-absence-of-.tldr: The paper develops a theory of objectives without inferior local minima and applies it to nonsmooth, nonconvex tensor decomposition.

paragraphs: Continuous-time Bayesian networks describe interacting entities whose states evolve over time. Learning their directed connections can reveal the structure of those interactions. Incomplete observations make this difficult because learning must account for unobserved dynamics, and simulating the full network process can become prohibitively complex as the system grows.

The paper introduces an approximation based on cluster-variational methods, drawing inspiration from statistical physics. Its purpose is to improve the treatment of the network dynamics beyond existing variational approximations while retaining scalability. This addresses a trade-off identified in the abstract: available sampling and low-order variational approaches can be expensive for large systems or insufficiently accurate.

The authors also analytically integrate out parameters of the approximate network, since the primary target is the connection structure rather than those parameters themselves. Together, these steps produce a method for learning structure directly from incomplete, noisy time series. The paper reports improved variational approximation and better scalability than existing methods, making the contribution relevant to network discovery when fully observed trajectories are unavailable.
neurips-2018-cluster-variational-approxi.tldr: Cluster-variational approximations enable scalable learning of continuous-time network structure from incomplete and noisy observations.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to generate graphs whose distribution resembles graphs observed during training, with molecule generation as its main application. It proposes a variational autoencoder in which both the encoder and decoder have graph structure. This makes the representation of relationships between entities part of the model on both sides of the encoding and generation process.

The decoder constructs a graph through an ordered sequence of extension steps. Introducing a sequence gives the generator a concrete construction process, but it also imposes an ordering on a graph. The authors discuss and analyze design choices intended to reduce potential disadvantages of that linearization. The ordering is therefore an explicit modeling decision whose consequences receive attention.

Experiments compare the method with a broad set of molecule-generation baselines and show that it matches important statistics of the original dataset. The authors also shape the latent space to support searching for molecules with desired properties. They demonstrate locally optimal designs, which supports property-directed generation without claiming that the search finds the globally best molecule.
neurips-2018-constrained-graph-variation.tldr: A graph-structured variational autoencoder generates molecules matching dataset statistics and supports locally optimal property-directed design.

paragraphs: Cubic-regularized Newton methods can produce second-order stationary solutions for nonconvex optimization, but understanding how quickly they converge requires information about the objective's geometry. This paper studies their asymptotic behavior using the Kurdyka–Lojasiewicz, or KL, property. The analysis therefore connects convergence speed to a mathematical property of the objective rather than treating all nonconvex functions alike.

The authors examine several ways to measure progress: the remaining objective-value gap, distance in the optimization variables, gradient size, and the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian. These quantities describe different aspects of approaching a stationary solution. Tracking all of them gives a broader account than studying only whether the objective value decreases.

The results characterize convergence behavior across the full parameter range of the KL property. Under that property, the derived asymptotic rates for cubic regularization are faster in order than those of first-order gradient descent algorithms. This is a comparison of asymptotic convergence rates under the stated geometric framework; it does not by itself assert a universal wall-clock advantage for every optimization problem.
neurips-2018-convergence-of-cubic-regula.tldr: Under the KL property, cubic regularization has asymptotic convergence rates that are order-wise faster than gradient descent.

paragraphs: Classification systems often need both accurate decisions and useful estimates of uncertainty. Gaussian process classification offers a principled way to obtain these, but its computational requirements can be difficult to sustain at large scale. This paper investigates whether the faster machinery of Gaussian process regression can provide a practical route to the same goal.

Directly treating classification labels as regression targets makes training faster, but the resulting predictions need calibration for classification and uncertainty estimation. The authors address this through a new construction of the regression labels. They interpret classification labels as coefficients of a degenerate Dirichlet distribution and use that interpretation to formulate the regression approach.

The experiments report essentially the same predictive accuracy and uncertainty quantification as Gaussian process classification while using only a fraction of its computational resources. The significance is that target construction can help connect an efficient regression procedure to a probabilistic classification task. The reported similarity is empirical and qualified as approximate, rather than an exact equivalence between the two models.
neurips-2018-dirichlet-based-gaussian-pr.tldr: Dirichlet-derived regression targets make Gaussian process classification substantially cheaper while empirically preserving similar accuracy and uncertainty quality.

paragraphs: Conventional embeddings represent each object as a point in a low-dimensional space. This paper extends that representation to elliptical probability distributions, whose equal-density contours have elliptical shapes. An object can therefore have both a location and a covariance structure, and the authors compare these representations using the 2-Wasserstein distance.

For the measures considered, the squared distance has a closed form combining differences between means with a Bures-metric term between covariance matrices. The covariance geometry also admits a suitable factor representation that behaves Euclideanly along the geodesic between matrices. These properties give the approach a computational foundation. When distributions collapse to point masses, their distance reduces to ordinary Euclidean distance, connecting the method directly to point embeddings.

The authors report more intuitive geometry and better numerical behavior than Gaussian embeddings based on Kullback–Leibler divergence. Their method also learns distributions with covariance matrices that need not be diagonal. Applications to visualization, word embeddings, and entailment or hypernymy illustrate how the richer representation can express relationships beyond the locations of isolated points.
neurips-2018-generalizing-point-embeddin.tldr: Wasserstein distances extend point embeddings to elliptical distributions with tractable geometry and support for non-diagonal covariance.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo methods use samples to support computation, but obtaining useful results can be challenging when the space has many dimensions and only a small number of samples is available. This paper investigates sampling in Euclidean spaces under those conditions. Its central move is to coordinate samples through dependence rather than requiring them to be independent.

The authors establish connections between this coupling of samples and optimal transport theory. Those connections lead to new sampling algorithms and provide theoretical explanations for existing strategies. The approach makes the relationship among samples part of the design problem, offering a geometric way to reason about how a limited collection of samples is arranged.

The paper compares the proposed strategies with earlier sample-efficiency methods, including quasi-Monte Carlo, through the study of discrepancy. It also explores their behavior empirically and observes benefits in reinforcement learning and generative modeling. These findings support coupled sampling as a useful strategy in the investigated settings, with both a theoretical foundation and evidence from applications.
neurips-2018-geometrically-coupled-monte.tldr: Geometrically coupling samples through optimal-transport ideas improves sampling strategies and shows empirical benefits in learning applications.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes can forecast, denoise, and help interpret long time series. State-space methods already make their cost linear in the number of observations, but computation remains cubic in the state dimension. This paper targets that remaining expense, which can prevent otherwise scalable temporal models from being practical.

The starting observation is that, with a Gaussian likelihood and regularly spaced observations, sufficiently long sequences can lead to a steady posterior state. The authors use this idea to formulate an infinite-horizon inference method for general likelihoods. Their scheme uses single-sweep expectation propagation, also called assumed density filtering, and reduces the per-observation dependence on state dimension from cubic to quadratic.

The method is also extended to learn hyperparameters online, allowing model adjustment during streaming inference. Examples include large but finite datasets and a smartphone demonstration processing a continuous stream updated at 100 Hz. The contribution combines a steady-state motivation with a practical approximate inference scheme, showing how reduced state-space computation can support real-time temporal modeling.
neurips-2018-infinite-horizon-gaussian-p.tldr: An infinite-horizon approximation reduces temporal Gaussian process inference to quadratic cost in state dimension per observation.

paragraphs: Persistence diagrams summarize the topology of complex data, but their geometry makes familiar learning operations difficult. In particular, computing an average diagram can be costly because these objects do not have the geometry of an ordinary inner-product space. This paper develops a tractable framework for distances, barycenters, and clustering directly with persistence diagrams.

The key step is to express diagram metrics as optimal transport problems. This opens access to computational methods developed for transport. On a planar grid, adding entropy regularization yields a convex problem that can be solved in linear time using the Sinkhorn algorithm and convolutions. The resulting computations can also stream on GPUs, supporting larger collections of diagrams.

The authors demonstrate clustering using diagram metrics on several thousand persistence diagrams, reporting a scale beyond earlier work in the literature. The contribution matters because it makes basic statistical operations more practical while retaining a connection to diagram geometry. Its computational route specifically relies on the grid-based, entropy-regularized transport formulation described in the abstract.
neurips-2018-large-scale-computation-of-.tldr: An entropy-regularized optimal transport framework scales persistence-diagram distances, averages, and clustering to thousands of diagrams.

paragraphs: Neural attention provides an effective, trainable approximation to alignment, but ordinary soft attention does not probabilistically sum over latent alignments. This complicates combining it with probabilistic models and inferring alignments after observing data. Hard attention offers a latent-variable alternative, yet the abstract identifies harder training and lower accuracy as practical obstacles.

The paper proposes variational attention networks that use amortized variational inference to learn latent alignment models with tighter approximation bounds. It also develops gradient variance-reduction methods to make training computationally feasible. Together, these components aim to preserve the probabilistic treatment of alignment while making its optimization more practical.

Experiments in machine translation and visual question answering show that exact latent-variable models outperform standard attention, although exact computation is inefficient. Training with hard attention loses those gains in the reported experiments. Variational attention retains most of the improvement while training at a speed comparable to neural attention. The result supports a practical middle ground between efficient soft attention and expensive exact latent-alignment inference.
neurips-2018-latent-alignment-and-variat.tldr: Variational attention preserves most observed gains from exact latent alignment while training at speeds comparable to standard attention.

paragraphs: The paper examines mental information gathering as sampling from a representation with separated clusters of concepts. Simple random-walk sampling has difficulty explaining two observed patterns: movement distances that follow a Lévy-flight distribution and slowly decaying, 1/f-like correlations over time. The authors seek one mechanism that can account for both patterns.

Their proposal uses Metropolis-coupled Markov chain Monte Carlo, or MC3, which runs multiple chains at different temperatures and exchanges their states. Heated chains move more readily between distant high-probability regions, while colder chains explore the current region locally. This combination fits the idea of a patchy mental representation containing multiple separated peaks.

The authors show that MC3 generates both Lévy-flight-like distances between consecutive samples and 1/f-like autocorrelations. This makes it a unified mechanistic account of the two phenomena that challenge simpler sampling models. The finding supports the proposed explanation through the patterns the algorithm produces; the abstract presents MC3 as a model of mental sampling rather than establishing that people literally implement this algorithm.
neurips-2018-mental-sampling-in-multimod.tldr: A coupled sampling model reproduces both long jumps and persistent temporal correlations observed in mental information gathering.

paragraphs: Different explanations reveal different aspects of a predictive model: examples provide reference cases, local explanations describe individual predictions, and global explanations reveal broader behavior. MAPLE aims to bring these perspectives together. It combines local linear modeling with random forests, interpreting the forests as both a way to define supervised neighborhoods and a way to select features.

MAPLE can explain another model as a black box, but it can also serve as the predictive model itself. In the latter role, its explanations describe its own prediction process faithfully. This matters because the explanation system and the predictor can be integrated, rather than requiring a separate account of how a prediction was made.

On several UCI datasets, MAPLE is reported to be at least as accurate as random forests and to produce more faithful local explanations than LIME. It also supplies example-based explanations and detects global patterns that help diagnose limitations in its local explanations. These results support combining predictive performance with several complementary forms of interpretability in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2018-model-agnostic-supervised-l.tldr: MAPLE combines local linear models and random forests to deliver accurate predictions with complementary, faithful explanations.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a tension in Bayesian learning: a statistical model can be useful even when it does not contain the true data-generating mechanism. In complex settings, assuming that the model is correct can be problematic. The authors propose a Bayesian nonparametric approach that uses statistical models without requiring them to be true.

The model still plays a constructive role. It can regularize nonparametric inference when only a small sample is available, supplying structure where the observations alone provide limited information. The approach can also correct approximate inference methods such as variational Bayes. This gives model-based information a role within a more flexible learning procedure.

The authors establish better theoretical properties than using a parametric model and provide a Monte Carlo sampling scheme designed for substantial scalability on modern computing architectures. Demonstrations include variational Bayes classifiers and Bayesian random forests. The contribution connects flexible inference, useful model structure, and scalable sampling, showing how an imperfect model can remain valuable without being treated as an exact description of the data.
neurips-2018-nonparametric-learning-from.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric approach uses statistical models for structure and regularization without assuming those models are true.

paragraphs: Maximum inner product search seeks dataset vectors with large inner products against a query. The paper identifies a weakness in SIMPLE-LSH, a leading hashing approach: long tails in the distribution of vector lengths can cause excessive normalization. The authors show that this affects both the method's theoretical behavior and its practical performance.

NORM-RANGING LSH addresses the issue by splitting the dataset into subsets and building an independent hash index for each. Partitioning changes the scope over which indexing and normalization operate, directly targeting the problem created by a long-tailed norm distribution. The paper also shows that dataset partitioning can improve another hashing-based method for maximum inner product search.

Under mild conditions, the authors prove lower query-time complexity than SIMPLE-LSH. Experiments show that the proposed method examines substantially fewer items while achieving the same recall. Keeping recall fixed makes the reported benefit especially clear: the method reduces search work at a comparable retrieval level. The theoretical improvement remains conditional on the assumptions of the result.
neurips-2018-norm-ranging-lsh-for-maximu.tldr: Partitioning vectors into separately indexed subsets improves inner-product search when long-tailed vector norms hinder normalization.

paragraphs: Choosing a word embedding's dimension determines how large its vector representation will be, but the best choice needs a principled way to compare embeddings. This paper proposes Pairwise Inner Product, or PIP, loss. Motivated by unitary invariance, it compares relationships encoded by embeddings rather than relying on their particular coordinate orientation.

Using matrix perturbation theory, the authors derive a bias–variance trade-off in the choice of dimension. The analysis explains why increasing representation size need not improve an embedding indefinitely and why an optimal dimension can exist. It also provides insight into when and how embeddings can resist overfitting, linking these behaviors to the same theoretical framework.

The paper then uses optimization of the PIP-loss trade-off to address dimensionality selection explicitly. Its contribution is both a comparison metric and an analysis that turns a representation-size choice into a mathematical optimization problem. The stated insights concern the conditions governing the trade-off, rather than asserting that one dimension is optimal for every embedding or that all large embeddings overfit.
neurips-2018-on-the-dimensionality-of-wo.tldr: PIP loss reveals a bias–variance trade-off that explains word-embedding behavior and provides a principled way to choose dimensionality.

paragraphs: Back-propagation can struggle to transmit useful learning signals through deep networks, yet design choices such as orthogonal initialization, batch normalization, and skip connections often help. This paper seeks a common explanation for that improvement. It views back-propagation through back-matching propagation, which minimizes a sequence of losses associated with individual network blocks.

The authors study the Hessian of each local back-matching loss, a matrix describing its curvature. They connect the spectrum of this local Hessian to the effectiveness of back-propagation and explain the listed design choices through improvements to that spectrum. This provides a block-level perspective on how network design affects the propagation of learning signals.

The same perspective suggests adjusting the relative training pace of different blocks. Using a scalar approximation to the local Hessian, the authors propose scale-amended SGD. Applied to networks with batch normalization, it produces favorable results compared with ordinary SGD. These experiments offer additional support for the relevance of local curvature, while the paper presents its analysis as a step toward understanding back-propagation's efficiency.
neurips-2018-on-the-local-hessian-in-bac.tldr: Local curvature helps explain effective back-propagation design choices and motivates an SGD variant that balances learning across network blocks.

paragraphs: Neural network optimization is difficult to analyze because its objective is generally nonconvex. This paper approaches the problem by restricting the network so that the optimization landscape has more tractable theoretical properties. For two-layer networks, it introduces Porcupine Neural Networks, whose weight vectors must lie along a finite collection of lines.

The restriction provides structure for studying local optima. The authors show that most local optima of the resulting optimization problems are global, and they characterize regions where inferior local optima may occur. This is a qualified landscape result: it identifies broad favorable behavior while retaining an explicit place for bad local solutions.

The paper also examines whether this constrained family can represent the behavior of unconstrained networks without excessive growth. Its theoretical and empirical results suggest that a polynomially large Porcupine Neural Network can approximate an unconstrained network. Together, the findings support structured network restrictions as a way to study optimization while retaining useful expressive capacity, rather than assuming that favorable landscape properties require abandoning approximation quality.
neurips-2018-porcupine-neural-networks-a.tldr: Constraining two-layer network weights to finitely many lines yields analyzable landscapes where most local optima are global.

paragraphs: Choosing a machine learning pipeline involves decisions about preprocessing, the predictive model, and hyperparameters. Evaluating these combinations can require substantial experimentation. This paper treats pipeline selection as a meta-learning problem: results from previous datasets provide information that can guide the search on another dataset.

The method combines collaborative filtering with Bayesian optimization. A probabilistic matrix factorization model transfers knowledge from experiments across hundreds of datasets, while an acquisition function chooses which pipelines to explore. These components connect learning from historical evaluations with making decisions about new evaluations, so the search can use more than the results obtained on the current dataset alone.

Experiments show that the approach quickly finds high-performing pipelines across a wide range of datasets and significantly outperforms the contemporary state of the art in those evaluations. The contribution is an integrated way to reuse accumulated experimentation and guide further search. Its reported advantage concerns how effectively the system identifies good pipelines, with performance evidence drawn from the paper's experiments.
neurips-2018-probabilistic-matrix-factor.tldr: Probabilistic matrix factorization transfers past pipeline results across datasets to guide efficient automated machine learning search.

paragraphs: REFUEL addresses online symptom checking as a reinforcement learning problem. The system must choose symptom questions that help it identify a disease efficiently. The paper focuses on improving those choices through two techniques, reward shaping and feature rebuilding, so that the learned policy can make better use of sparse symptom information.

Reward shaping guides the search for a policy toward more useful directions. Feature rebuilding encourages the agent to learn correlations among features. The two mechanisms therefore contribute different kinds of guidance: one shapes policy learning, while the other develops knowledge of relationships among symptoms. Together, they can identify questions that a patient is likely to answer positively.

The reported experiments show that combining these techniques lets the symptom checker identify disease more rapidly and accurately. This connects the quality of question selection with the effectiveness of the overall diagnostic interaction. The stated result is an experimental improvement for the symptom-checking method, with the contribution centered on how reward design and feature relationships support learning which questions to ask.
neurips-2018-refuel-exploring-sparse-fea.tldr: REFUEL combines reward shaping and feature rebuilding to learn symptom queries that improve diagnostic speed and accuracy in experiments.

paragraphs: Distributed training can be limited by communication between devices rather than by computation alone. Sending only a few gradient entries reduces that traffic, but it also leaves information out of each update. This paper analyzes sparse or compressed stochastic gradient descent, including strategies that keep the largest entries or select entries randomly.

The central addition is memory that records accumulated compression errors. With this error compensation, the authors show that the analyzed scheme converges at the same rate as ordinary SGD. Remembering omitted information is therefore essential to the stated result: the guarantee applies to compression equipped with compensation, rather than compression considered on its own.

The analysis shows that communication can be reduced by a factor equal to the problem's dimension, and sometimes more, while retaining the convergence rate. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical findings and good scalability in distributed applications. The contribution gives theoretical support to a practical communication-saving strategy, explaining how retaining compression errors can preserve optimization progress even when each transmitted update is much smaller.
neurips-2018-sparsified-sgd-with-memory-.tldr: Remembering accumulated compression errors lets sparsified SGD retain ordinary SGD's convergence rate while sharply reducing communication.

paragraphs: Data collected across multiple modalities can be organized into tensors, which extend matrices to more dimensions. Low-rank decomposition looks for a simpler underlying structure within them. This paper studies the algorithmic behavior of that recovery problem when the low-rank tensor is obscured by noise, including tensors with arbitrary shapes.

The authors derive Bayesian approximate message passing algorithms and use dynamic mean field theory to characterize their performance precisely. The theory reveals transitions between easy, hard, and impossible inference regimes. Distinguishing these regimes matters because the difficulty of recovering structure changes across the analyzed settings, rather than following one uniform pattern.

The theoretical predictions closely match simulations, and the analysis reveals qualitative differences from symmetric, cubic tensor decomposition. This shows why conclusions drawn from that special shape may miss behavior in more general tensors. The paper also compares approximate message passing with alternating least squares, reporting that message passing significantly outperforms it in the presence of noise. The work combines algorithm design, predictive theory, and empirical comparison.
neurips-2018-statistical-mechanics-of-lo.tldr: Bayesian message passing and statistical-mechanics theory reveal recovery regimes for noisy low-rank tensors and strong performance against alternating least squares.

paragraphs: The paper studies maximizing deep submodular functions under a matroid constraint. This function class includes facility location, weighted coverage, and sums of concave functions applied to modular functions as strict subfamilies. Its breadth makes an efficient optimization method useful across several forms of structured subset selection.

The authors build on the continuous greedy perspective but identify a computationally accessible concave relaxation of the multilinear extension for any deep submodular function. They optimize that relaxation using gradient ascent, then use pipage rounding to recover a discrete solution. This separates an efficiently handled continuous optimization problem from the step that produces the selected subset.

The approximation guarantee depends on the matroid rank and accuracy parameters and is often better than the standard 1−1/e guarantee. The stated running time is O(n²/ε²), plus rounding time, and the method is reported to run much faster than continuous greedy. The bound also applies to fully curved functions, where a curvature-based guarantee returns to 1−1/e. Computational experiments support the theoretical results.
neurips-2018-submodular-maximization-via.tldr: A tractable concave relaxation enables fast gradient-based maximization of deep submodular functions with often stronger approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: Optimization methods are often assessed by counting gradient computations, implicitly treating each computation as a fresh expense. This paper studies a more detailed cost model: after computing a gradient at one point, some of that work may remain useful at later points. The authors call this persistence the lingering of gradients.

They show how exploiting lingering can improve the running time of gradient descent and SVRG. One result assumes that the additional work needed for gradients scales linearly with the distance traveled. Under that condition, gradient descent's convergence rate in the refined computational accounting can improve from 1/T to exp(−T^(1/3)). The condition is central to that comparison.

The empirical study considers a hypothetical revenue-management problem using the Yahoo! Front Page Today Module application with 4.6 million users. It reaches 10⁻⁶ error, or 10⁻¹² dual error, in six passes through the dataset. The contribution highlights reusable gradient computation as a source of efficiency that a simple count of complete gradient evaluations can overlook.
neurips-2018-the-lingering-of-gradients-.tldr: Reusing lingering gradient information improves optimization runtime, with faster conditional convergence under a distance-sensitive computation model.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised classification uses unlabeled observations alongside labeled examples. This paper asks whether adding those observations can come with a guarantee of improvement over the supervised classifier. It studies linear classifiers defined through convex margin-based surrogate losses, with improvement measured using that surrogate on both the labeled and unlabeled data.

For losses that decrease with the margin, the authors prove an impossibility result: no semi-supervised approach can provide the specified improvement guarantee. The scope of this result matters. It addresses a guarantee under the stated classifier and loss conditions, rather than claiming that unlabeled data can never help empirically or under a different evaluation criterion.

The authors then show that safe improvements are possible for convex margin-based losses that also have increasing behavior. Thus, the shape of the surrogate loss changes what can be guaranteed from unlabeled data. The contribution identifies both a negative boundary and a positive possibility within a closely related family of learning objectives, making loss selection part of the theoretical foundation for safe semi-supervised learning.
neurips-2018-the-pessimistic-limits-and-.tldr: Guaranteed semi-supervised improvement is impossible for decreasing convex margin losses in the studied setting, but possible for losses that also increase.
